units.translation: 974. καλαύροπα: instead of καλόροπον, a herdsman's staff. Homer (Iliad 23.845): 'a herdsman's staff'.

982-92a. "There is a certain island before the strait ... in the sea": the sense of these words is this: as they sail into the Ionian gulf, there is a well-harbored and fertile island, under which they say the sickle of Cronus lies, with which he cut off his father's genitals. Others say it belongs to Demeter,
with which she taught the Titans to reap grain; for the goddess then dwelt on that island, having come to love Macris. ... which the Phaeacians inhabited, being of divine descent.
b. παροιτέρη: in front. Lᵍ P
c. ἀμφιλαφής: having anchorage on both sides.

d. 〈πορθμοῖο παροιτέρη Ἰονίοιο:〉 [and] the Ionian sea, because it separates Italy from Epirus. 〈Κεραυνίη δὲ ἅλς . . .〉 In it lies the island Corcyra; this was formerly called Scheria. He has called the harbor ἀμφιλαφῆ, meaning having anchorage on both sides, which Callimachus (fr. 336 Schn.) called ἀμφίδυμον. Historically, Apollonius says the harbor is ἀμφιλαφῆ, having anchorage on all sides; Apollonides in his Periplus of Europe (M. IV 309) gives an account of the harbor of the Phaeacians.
e. Some rendered ἀμφιλαφής as meaning 'woody'; to which πίειρα is appropriately joined, clearly meaning 'rich' and 'fertile'. P

g. 〈νῆσος,〉 ᾗ ὕπο δὴ κεῖσθαι δρέπ〈ανον〉: [the] island Corcyra; this was formerly called Scheria. Aristotle in his Constitution of the Corcyraeans (fr. 469 Rose 1555a35) gives the reason: he says that Demeter, fearing that the rivers coming from the mainland might make it part of the mainland, begged Poseidon to turn aside the streams of the rivers; when these were checked, it was named Scheria instead of Drepane. ... because Demeter asked for a sickle

from Hephaestus to teach the Titans to reap, and then hid it in the coastal part of the island; and as the sea washed over it, the appearance of the land became like a sickle. Timaeus (fr. 54 M. I 203) says that the sickle with which Zeus cut off the genitals of Cronus [or Uranus] was hidden there.
h. Macris from Macris, the nurse of Dionysus, and Corcyra from Corcyra, the daughter of Asopus. P

i. στάχυν ὄμπνιον: abundant, plentiful. Philetas in his Miscellaneous Glosses (fr. 44 Kuchenmueller) rendered ὄμπνιον στάχυν as 'juicy and nourishing'. Some of the Cyrenaeans call the rich and prosperous ὄμπνιον. But it is better to say 'life-giving', as if it were 'breathing' and 'nourishing'.
